exam_points: Thalidomide: untested teratogen, withdrawn 26 November 1961; now used in myeloma and leprosy.
LD₅₀: dose killing 50% of animals; lower LD₅₀ = more toxic.
LC₅₀ is used for inhalation (mg/L or ppm).
Acute studies: rodents, ~5/sex/dose, 14-day observation.
3Rs: Replace, Reduce, Refine.
Limit test at 2,000 mg/kg replaces full LD₅₀ tests.
Repeated dose: 28 days, 90 days, ≥ 6 months; key output NOAEL.
Genotoxicity battery: Ames, mammalian cell assay, in vivo micronucleus.
Ames: histidine-dependent Salmonella, with and without S9.
Micronucleus detects clastogens and aneugens.
IARC group 1: tobacco, asbestos, aflatoxins.
Carcinogenicity studies last 18-24 months in rodents.

deeper.title: Why thalidomide changed drug regulation
deeper.html:
Thalidomide looked safe in the tests of its time, which did not examine pregnant animals. Thousands of children were born with limb defects before the link was made. The disaster led regulators to require embryo-fetal development studies before approval, which is exactly the reproductive toxicity testing this lecture describes.

Source: the lecture's thalidomide slides.

deeper.title: Why the Ames test uses liver extract
deeper.html:
Many carcinogens, such as benzopyrene, are harmless until liver enzymes convert them into reactive metabolites. Bacteria lack these enzymes, so a test without them would miss such compounds. Adding S9, the liver microsome fraction, lets the test catch substances that become mutagenic only after metabolism.

Source: the lecture's Ames test slides.

exam_points: Paracelsus: the dose makes the poison.
Toxicants are synthetic; toxins are natural.
Toxicokinetics = ADME; toxicodynamics = target and effect.
Functional toxicant: blood level parallels severity. Morphological: delayed, silent start.
Paracetamol: Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 to 24 h.
Paraquat: pulmonary fibrosis.
Acids → coagulative necrosis (superficial); alkalis → liquefactive necrosis (deeper).
Organophosphates inhibit AChE → cholinergic toxidrome; antidote pralidoxime.
CO binds Hb 210× more than O₂; treat with oxygen (normobaric or hyperbaric).
HbCO 60-70% is fatal.
PPD (Takaout Roumia): oedema, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, methaemoglobinaemia.
Antagonism is the basis of antidotes.

deeper.title: Why CO kills even at low air concentrations
deeper.html:
Because haemoglobin binds CO 210 times more avidly than oxygen, even a small fraction of CO in the air gradually occupies a large share of haemoglobin. The bound haemoglobin also holds its remaining oxygen more tightly, so tissues receive even less. Headache and confusion in several family members in winter should always make you think of CO.

Source: the lecture's carbon monoxide slides.

deeper.title: Why morphological toxicants are dangerous despite a quiet start
deeper.html:
Paracetamol and paraquat injure cells through reactive metabolites and free radicals, and the damage takes hours to days to show. A patient who looks well after an overdose may already be heading for liver failure or lung fibrosis. That is why the paracetamol nomogram uses the blood level and time, not symptoms, to decide on treatment.

Source: the lecture's functional vs morphological toxicant slides.

exam_points: ADME: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion.
Passive diffusion is the main mechanism (Fick's law).
Facilitated diffusion and active transport are saturable; active uses ATP.
P-glycoprotein is an ABC efflux pump, key at the BBB.
F = AUC oral / AUC IV.
Only un-ionised, lipophilic forms cross membranes.
Protein binding lowers immediate toxicity but prolongs intoxication.
Weak bases are trapped in cells (ion trapping).
Paracetamol → NAPQI (phase I), neutralised by glutathione (phase II).
Inducers: smoking, alcohol, rifampicin; inhibitors: grapefruit, ketoconazole.
Alkaline urine increases excretion of weak acids (salicylates).
t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL; steady state after 4-5 half-lives.
Zero-order: alcohol, high-dose aspirin.
Post-mortem: sample femoral blood and vitreous humour, not cardiac blood.

deeper.title: Why cardiac blood misleads after death
deeper.html:
Lipophilic drugs with a large volume of distribution are concentrated in the lungs, liver and heart muscle. After death, circulation stops and they diffuse back into the nearby blood, so blood drawn from the heart can show several times the level present in life. Peripheral femoral blood, far from these reservoirs, stays closer to the true value, which is why the lecture's cases were reclassified from overdose to therapeutic use.

Source: the lecture's post-mortem redistribution cases.

deeper.title: Why alkalinising the urine helps in aspirin poisoning
deeper.html:
Salicylic acid is a weak acid. In alkaline urine most of it is ionised, and ionised molecules cannot diffuse back through the tubular wall. It is therefore trapped in the urine and excreted, instead of being reabsorbed. This is ion trapping used as a treatment.

Source: the lecture's tubular reabsorption slide.

exam_points: Methaemoglobin: Fe³⁺, cannot carry O₂; chocolate-brown blood; SpO₂ ≈ 85%.
MetHb causes: dapsone, benzocaine, lidocaine, nitrates/nitrites, aniline.
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
CO: pulse oximetry falsely normal; co-oximetry is the gold standard.
COHb half-life: 4-6 h in air, 60-90 min on 100% O₂.
Hyperbaric O₂ if COHb > 25% (> 15% pregnancy), neuro signs, cardiac ischaemia.
Lead: microcytic anaemia, basophilic stippling (inhibits δ-ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase).
G6PD deficiency: bite cells, Heinz bodies; triggers dapsone, primaquine, fava beans.
Clozapine → agranulocytosis; chloramphenicol → aplastic anaemia; benzene → pancytopenia.
Warfarin/rodenticides block vitamin K recycling (II, VII, IX, X).
High anion gap: methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, iron, metformin, cyanide, CO.
Rhabdomyolysis: CK > 5× normal, dark urine, AKI; IV fluids ± alkalinisation.

deeper.title: Why oxygen does not fix methaemoglobinaemia cyanosis
deeper.html:
The problem is not a lack of oxygen in the lungs but haemoglobin that cannot hold it: ferric iron simply does not bind O₂. Giving more oxygen raises the dissolved PaO₂ but cannot convert Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺. Methylene blue does that chemically, which is why it, not oxygen, is the treatment.

Source: the lecture's methaemoglobinaemia slides.

deeper.title: Why methylene blue can harm G6PD-deficient patients
deeper.html:
Methylene blue works by using NADPH to reduce methaemoglobin. G6PD is the enzyme that makes NADPH in red cells, so in G6PD deficiency the drug has nothing to work with, and it acts as an oxidant instead, triggering haemolysis. The lecture therefore lists G6PD deficiency both as a contraindication and as a trigger category.

Source: the lecture's treatment and G6PD slides.
